user_proposal: This clinical trial is a phase 2, adaptive, randomized controlled trial designed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of TB31F in reducing Plasmodium falciparum transmission in malaria-naive adults in Mali. The trial will involve four treatment arms with different dosing regimens, and participants will be randomly assigned to one of the arms based on their response to the initial dose. The study duration is expected to be 12 months, with regular follow-up visits and assessments. Key inclusion/exclusion criteria include age between 18-50 years, malaria-negative status, and no prior treatment for P. falciparum infection. Primary objectives include evaluating the safety and efficacy of TB31F in reducing P. falciparum transmission, as well as assessing the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the drug.
mechanism: TB31F is a monoclonal antibody targeting the Plasmodium falciparum neonatal receptor (PNR), which plays a crucial role in the parasite's ability to infect red blood cells. The mechanism of action involves binding to PNR, thereby blocking the parasite's entry into red blood cells and reducing transmission. Preclinical studies have shown that TB31F is effective in reducing P. falciparum transmission in animal models, and the drug has been designed to have a long circulation half-life and favorable pH-dependent binding to human neonatal receptor.
biomarker: Primary biomarkers include Plasmodium falciparum antigen levels, hemoglobin levels, and liver enzymes. Secondary biomarkers include inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein and interleukin-6. Exploratory biomarkers include genetic markers associated with P. falciparum resistance to TB31F. Biomarker measurement methods include enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), real-time PCR, and mass spectrometry. Biomarker validation status includes in vitro and in vivo validation of the primary biomarkers.
endpoint: Primary endpoints include the proportion of participants achieving at least 80% reduction in P. falciparum transmission, as well as the mean reduction in P. falciparum antigen levels. Secondary endpoints include the incidence of adverse events, laboratory abnormalities, and changes in hemoglobin levels. Exploratory endpoints include the effect of TB31F on inflammatory markers and genetic markers associated with P. falciparum resistance. Endpoint measurement methods include standard membrane feeding assay (SMFA), real-time PCR, and ELISA. Endpoint validation status includes statistical analysis plan for primary and secondary endpoints.
indication: Target disease/condition: Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Disease severity/stage: Mild to moderate P. falciparum infection. Patient population: Malaria-naive adults aged 18-50 years. Prior treatment requirements: None. Disease-specific criteria include age, malaria-negative status, and no prior treatment for P. falciparum infection.
safety: Known safety concerns include anaphylaxis, allergic reactions, and infusion-related reactions. Risk factors include pre-existing medical conditions such as hypertension and diabetes. Safety monitoring plan includes regular assessment of vital signs, laboratory parameters, and adverse events. Adverse event collection will be performed using a standardized adverse event reporting form. Safety stopping rules will be established based on the incidence of adverse events. Risk mitigation strategies include dose reduction or discontinuation in case of severe adverse events.

Subjects must have been treated with antiretrovirals for at least 6 months and be failing or had recently failed (i.e., in the last 8 weeks) therapy.
The trial was composed of three discrete periods:
• Control period (Day 0 to Day 6): Subjects were either monitored on their current failing therapy or received no therapy if they had failed and discontinued treatment within the 8 weeks preceding screening. This was an observational period to establish baseline HIV viral load.
• Functional monotherapy period (Day 7 to Day 13): All subjects received a 2,000 mg loading dose of TROGARZO on Day 7. Subjects on a failing ART regimen continued to receive their failing regimen in addition to the loading dose of TROGARZO. This period was to establish the virologic activity of TROGARZO.
• Maintenance period (Day 14 to Week 25): On Day 14 of the treatment period, viral load was assessed for the primary endpoint, and thereafter the background regimen was optimized to include at least one drug to which the subject’s virus was susceptible. The use of an investigational drug(s) as a component of the optimized background regimen was allowed. Beginning at Day 21, an 800 mg maintenance dose of TROGARZO was administered every two weeks through Week 25. This period was to establish the safety and durability of virologic suppression of TROGARZO when used in combination with an optimized background regimen.
The majority of subjects in Trial TMB-301 were male (85%), white (55%) and between 23 and 65 years of age (mean [SD] age: 50.5 [11.0] years). At Baseline, median viral load and CD4+ T cell counts were 35,350 copies/mL and 73 cells/mm3, respectively. The subjects were heavily treatment-experienced: 53% of participants had been treated with 10 or more antiretroviral drugs prior to trial enrollment; 98% percent had been treated with NRTIs, 98% with PIs, 80% with NNRTIs, 78% with INSTIs, 30% with gp41 fusion inhibitors, and 20% with CCR5 co-receptor antagonists.
The primary efficacy endpoint was the proportion of subjects achieving a ≥ 0.5 log10 decrease in viral load from the beginning to the end of the “Functional monotherapy period” as compared to the proportion of subjects achieving a ≥ 0.5 log10 decrease from the beginning to the end of the “Control period”, as defined above. Discontinuation and Infusion Rate Adjustments in the PALM Trial
Approximately 99% of subjects who received INMAZEB in the PALM trial were able to complete their dose within three hours. Two subjects who received INMAZEB (1%) did not receive their complete infusion. One of the two subjects did not complete their INMAZEB infusion because of fever elevation [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1)].

final_review_paragraph:
The proposed phase 2, adaptive, randomized controlled trial for evaluating the safety and efficacy of TB31F in reducing Plasmodium falciparum transmission in malaria-naive adults in Mali has been reviewed. The proposed mechanism of action involves binding to PNR, thereby blocking the parasite's entry into red blood cells, which is similar to INMAZEB. However, to ensure a comprehensive understanding of TB31F's effectiveness and safety, the following recommendations have been made.

A risk assessment indicates that the mechanism of action is low-risk, given preclinical studies demonstrating its efficacy in reducing P. falciparum transmission. However, it is essential to investigate alternative targets for TB31F to provide similar binding affinity and blocking activity against PNR, as part of an ongoing effort to improve our understanding of this approach.

In terms of biomarkers, the use of parasite density, viral load, or CD4+ T cell counts can help monitor the efficacy of TB31F in reducing malaria transmission. Nonetheless, novel biomarkers that could provide earlier or more sensitive detection of malaria infection or transmission are recommended to be explored as part of an alternative pathway.

The primary endpoint for this trial should be the proportion of subjects experiencing a reduction in malaria transmission, which is similar to the approach used in INMAZEB. However, considering multiple endpoints such as incidence rate of malaria, mortality rate, or quality of life assessments could provide a more comprehensive understanding of TB31F's effectiveness and safety.

Furthermore, it is crucial to ensure that the safety profile of TB31F is comparable to that of INMAZEB, with most adverse events being mild and transient. Alternative formulations or delivery methods for TB31F are recommended to be investigated as an alternative pathway to reduce the risk of adverse events or improve its tolerability.

Given these considerations, it is recommended that the proposed clinical trial proceed with caution while incorporating these recommendations into the study protocol. Regular monitoring of participants' safety and efficacy will be essential to ensure the successful completion of this trial.

In conclusion, the proposed phase 2, adaptive, randomized controlled trial for evaluating the safety and efficacy of TB31F in reducing Plasmodium falciparum transmission in malaria-naive adults in Mali has been reviewed. With these recommendations in mind, we can work towards ensuring a more comprehensive understanding of TB31F's effectiveness and safety.

Mitigation Strategy:
1. Investigate alternative targets for TB31F to provide similar binding affinity and blocking activity against PNR.
2. Explore novel biomarkers that could provide earlier or more sensitive detection of malaria infection or transmission.
3. Consider using multiple endpoints such as incidence rate of malaria, mortality rate, or quality of life assessments to provide a more comprehensive understanding of TB31F's effectiveness.
4. Investigate alternative formulations or delivery methods for TB31F to reduce the risk of adverse events or improve its tolerability.
5. Regularly monitor participants' safety and efficacy during the trial.
6. Continue to conduct ongoing clinical trials and studies to further assess the safety and efficacy of TB31F in reducing Plasmodium falciparum transmission in malaria-naive adults in Mali.
7. Provide a comprehensive risk management plan that outlines the potential risks and mitigations for each of these recommendations.
8. Obtain regulatory approvals and clearance from relevant authorities before proceeding with the trial.
9. Ensure compliance with Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guidelines throughout the trial.
10. Establish a system for continuous monitoring and evaluation of the trial's progress to ensure its successful completion.

Regulatory Approvals:
1. Obtain approval from the Institutional Review Board (IRB) prior to enrolling participants in the trial.
2. Obtain clearance from the relevant authorities, such as the FDA or equivalent regulatory bodies in other countries.
3. Comply with all applicable regulations and guidelines, including but not limited to GCP, ICH-GCP, and local laws and regulations.
4. Provide regular reports to the IRB and regulatory authorities on the trial's progress.
5. Ensure that all participants are fully informed about the risks and benefits of the trial and provide their signed informed consent before enrolling in the trial.

Conclusion:
In conclusion, this regulatory review has provided a comprehensive assessment of the proposed phase 2, adaptive, randomized controlled trial for evaluating the safety and efficacy of TB31F in reducing Plasmodium falciparum transmission in malaria-naive adults in Mali. The recommendations made during this review have been outlined above and are intended to ensure a more comprehensive understanding of TB31F's effectiveness and safety.

1. Proceed with caution while incorporating the recommended modifications into the study protocol.
2. Regularly monitor participants' safety and efficacy during the trial.
3. Continue to conduct ongoing clinical trials and studies to further assess the safety and efficacy of TB31F in reducing Plasmodium falciparum transmission in malaria-naive adults in Mali.
4. Provide a comprehensive risk management plan that outlines the potential risks and mitigations for each of these recommendations.
